rounds.answer: The retrieved evidence does not support this claim, and none of the supplied items actually address whether an agent reviewing its own work is treated as sufficient quality control. One clip explicitly points the other way: it states that frontier models 'can pretty much do anything, but you need to review the decisions,' implying that human (not self-) review is needed rather than self-review being sufficient. Other evidence touches on related but distinct topics: post-training as a human-driven refinement phase for LLM quality and alignment, a model splitting itself into departments including a 'quality control' function (described anecdotally, without evaluating whether this self-organized QC was adequate), humans deleting/editing an agent's memory context to keep it behaving 'consistently,' and a builder's account of personally validating AI-generated code (i.e., a human reviewing the agent's work, not the agent reviewing itself). None of these establish a consistent narrative in the corpus that self-review by an agent is described as sufficient quality control.
